questions.answer: θ0 = 0 so sin θ0 = 0, and s0 and s1 divide by zero (NaN); rounding can also push the cosine above 1, making arccos NaN. Clip the cosine to [−1, 1] and fall back to linear interpolation when sin θ0 is tiny.
questions.explanation: An edge case of the printed code; not discussed in the book.

questions.question: Without looking, can you write slerp in one line of math and say what happens at t = 0 and t = 1?
questions.answer: slerp(t) = sin((1−t)θ0)/sin θ0 · v1 + sin(tθ0)/sin θ0 · v2; t = 0 gives v1, t = 1 gives v2.
questions.explanation: At t = 0 the weights are (1, 0), at t = 1 they are (0, 1).

questions.question: According to the page, why is linear interpolation between two text embeddings undesirable?
options: It is too slow to compute on a GPU
Its intermediate points land inside the sphere, off the manifold where embeddings are meaningful to the denoiser
It can only interpolate between exactly two prompts
It changes the negative prompt embeddings
questions.answer: Its intermediate points land inside the sphere, off the manifold where embeddings are meaningful to the denoiser
questions.explanation: The page says linear interpolation 'would land us inside the sphere' and that we want to stay on the manifold's surface where points have meaning for the denoiser. Lerp is cheap, slerp also handles exactly two points, and neither method touches the negative-prompt entries (they are copied from e1 in Listing 17.10).

questions.question: Two unit-norm embeddings are orthogonal. What are the norms of the lerp midpoint and of the slerp midpoint (t = 0.5)?
questions.answer: Lerp: about 0.707 (1/√2). Slerp: 1.
questions.explanation: Lerp gives 0.5·v1 + 0.5·v2 with norm √(0.25+0.25) = 0.707. Slerp with θ0 = π/2 gives weights sin(π/4)/sin(π/2) ≈ 0.707 each, so the norm is √(0.5+0.5) = 1.

questions.question: What values of t does interpolate_text_embeddings(e1, e2, start=0.5, stop=0.6, num=9) use, and why did the authors choose this range?
questions.answer: t = 0.5, 0.5125, 0.525, ..., 0.6 (nine evenly spaced values, step 0.0125). The range zooms in on the middle of the interpolation, where the morph becomes visually obvious.
questions.explanation: interpolate_text_embeddings uses np.linspace(start, stop, num) (p.559). The text and callout say the window zooms into the middle of the [0, 1] interpolation.

questions.question: The authors admit the text-embedding manifold is not a sphere. Why is slerp still justified?
questions.answer: The manifold is a smooth surface of vectors with roughly the same magnitude, so it is sphere-like. Interpolating along a sphere preserves that magnitude and is a better approximation than a straight line, which shrinks the norm in the middle.
questions.explanation: This is the argument of the second paragraph: sphere-like is enough for slerp to beat lerp, even though slerp does not follow the true curvature.

questions.question: Why does figure 17.17 show a single coherent creature in the middle frames instead of a double-exposure of a dog and a monster?
questions.answer: Each frame is generated from scratch by the diffusion model, conditioned on one intermediate embedding. The model maps that in-between point on the text manifold to a coherent image; it never blends pixels.
questions.explanation: The loop calls denoise_with_text_embeddings(et) for each interpolated et. Interpolation happens in the conditioning (latent) space, not in pixel space; compare figure 5.8 on p.169.

questions.question: Which parts of the embedding tuple are interpolated in this experiment?
options: All four tensors
Only the negative prompt's sequence and vector
Only the positive prompt's sequence (index 0) and pooled vector (index 2)
Only the pooled vectors of both prompts
questions.answer: Only the positive prompt's sequence (index 0) and pooled vector (index 2)
questions.explanation: Listing 17.10 slerps e1[0]/e2[0] and e1[2]/e2[2] and copies e1[1] and e1[3], the negative-prompt entries, which the callout says are unused. 'Only pooled vectors' misses the sequence, and the other options interpolate the wrong entries.

questions.question: Could you explain figure 17.16 to a friend in two sentences, including what the green chord and the orange arc points represent?
questions.answer: The circle is the embedding manifold, the endpoints are two prompt embeddings. The green chord's points (lerp) fall inside the circle, off the manifold, while slerp's points along the arc stay on the surface where the denoiser expects its inputs.
questions.explanation: If you can state this and why 'on the surface' matters (in-distribution conditioning), you have the page's key idea.

questions.question: Which statement matches the chapter summary's description of diffusion models?
options: They learn a structured latent space mainly used for face swapping
They generate by repeatedly denoising an image starting from pure noise
They train a generator against a discriminator
They can only be conditioned on class labels
questions.answer: They generate by repeatedly denoising an image starting from pure noise
questions.explanation: That is the summary's wording. Structured latent spaces for editing are attributed to VAEs; generator-vs-discriminator describes GANs; the summary says diffusion models are easily conditioned on text captions, not just labels.

questions.question: Name the three major tools for deep-learning image generation listed in the summary.
questions.answer: VAEs, diffusion models and GANs.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first summary bullet. The chapter implements VAEs and diffusion models; GANs are only mentioned (p.534).

questions.question: What do the authors mean by 'deep neural networks are interpolation machines', and how does the prompt-morphing experiment illustrate it?
questions.answer: Networks map complex real-world distributions onto smooth, low-dimensional manifolds and generalize by moving between known examples on them. In the experiment, walking between two prompts' text embeddings yields a continuous sequence of valid in-between images, so the learned mapping is smooth and interpolative.
questions.explanation: This combines the opening paragraph with summary bullet 5 and the theory of chapter 5 (p.169).

questions.question: Which property of VAEs makes them well suited to latent-space animations, according to the summary?
options: Their outputs are the most photorealistic
Their latent representations are highly structured and continuous
They need no training data
They use text embeddings as input
questions.answer: Their latent representations are highly structured and continuous
questions.explanation: The summary credits VAEs' structured, continuous latent spaces. Photorealism is credited to diffusion models; VAEs do need training data and are not inherently text-conditioned.

questions.question: Given chapter 5's view of interpolation, what limitation should you expect even from a powerful text-to-image model?
questions.answer: Interpolation gives only local generalization. The model can blend concepts well represented in its training data, but it does not understand the physical world, so it can produce errors such as extra fingers or implausible poses for unusual combinations.
questions.explanation: p.169 says interpolation enables local generalization only; p.534 gives examples of coherence failures.

questions.question: Without looking, can you list the five summary points of chapter 17 and point to the section where each was developed?
questions.answer: Latent spaces and the three families (17.1); VAEs (17.1.2-17.1.3); diffusion models (17.2); Stable Diffusion 3 (17.3); interpolative latent space of text-to-image models (17.3.1).
questions.explanation: If you can match each bullet to its section, you have a solid map of the chapter.
